clue.text: See 23
Clumsily runs poll in The Sun that's sent up

indicators.note: one word sits in another, so the vote goes inside the newspaper's name
in a down clue, sent up means the whole thing is read from bottom to top

blocks.note: Sol is the Latin name of the sun
taken as written

explanation.surface: A newspaper's opinion poll gets mocked for being clumsily run.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Sun' looks like the tabloid that prints the poll, but it is the Latin sun god's name.
explanation.definitionFit: To lollop is to move with ungainly bounding strides, so a clumsy runner lollops.

clue.text: Firm having to restrict Corbynite principles?

indicators.note: to restrict something is to hem it in, so the firm closes around the other word

blocks.note: Co. is the abbreviation for company
a follower of left-winger Jeremy Corbyn is a red

explanation.surface: A company forced to rein in its left-wing beliefs.
explanation.walkthrough: Jeremy Corbyn led the UK Labour Party from 2015 to 2020 from its left wing.
explanation.definitionFit: A credo is a statement of belief, the set of principles someone lives by.

clue.text: Conclude negative vote leads to hellish place

blocks.note: to infer is to conclude from evidence
a vote against

explanation.surface: Deciding a 'no' vote opens the road to ruin.
explanation.definitionFit: An inferno is a raging blaze, and Dante's Inferno is his name for hell itself.

clue.text: Standards of Lamont, St John-Stevas and Tebbit?

blocks.note: first meaning: accepted standards or rules
second meaning: all three Tory politicians were called Norman, shortened to Norm

explanation.surface: Asking what moral standards three Thatcher-era Conservative ministers held.
explanation.walkthrough: Norman Lamont, Norman St John-Stevas and Norman Tebbit were all Conservative cabinet ministers; Norm is short for Norman.
explanation.definitionFit: Norms are usual patterns or expected standards of behaviour, and the plural of the nickname gives the same word.

clue.text: Herculean task for party dominating ballot?

blocks.note: first meaning: one of the twelve ... of Hercules
second meaning: the UK political party expected to win the vote

explanation.surface: Winning an election outright is a mighty job for any political party.
explanation.walkthrough: The puzzle appeared during the 2024 UK general election campaign, when the Labour Party led the polls.
explanation.definitionFit: Hercules performed twelve labours, and Labour is the British centre-left party then leading the polls.

clue.text: Liberal excluded is hard and coarse

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for Liberal
left out
taken as written
H for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A Liberal politician shut out of things turns hard and crude.
explanation.definitionFit: A lout is a rough, ill-mannered man, so loutish behaviour is coarse and boorish.

clue.text: British have nowhere to swim, but big swing here?

blocks.note: B is the abbreviation for British
split 'nowhere' as 'no where': to lack is to have none, and a pool is where one swims

explanation.surface: Britain has nowhere to go swimming, yet there is a big swing somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nowhere' must be split into 'no where'. Blackpool is a Lancashire seaside resort whose South seat saw a huge swing to Labour in the May 2024 by-election.
explanation.definitionFit: The resort is known for fairground rides, and its 2024 by-election produced one of the largest voter swings ever seen.

clue.text: Really poor — so save?

blocks.note: first meaning: very bad, ineffective
second meaning, read as two words: to save, consume a smaller amount

explanation.surface: Someone truly hard up is told to put money aside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poor' suggests lacking money, but the sense is of poor quality; the second half splits the answer into two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Something useless is worthless or very bad, and 'use less' is exactly what saving means.

clue.text: Sad Tory

blocks.note: first meaning: feeling down
second meaning: the Conservative Party colour

explanation.walkthrough: In Britain the Conservatives (Tories) are associated with the colour blue.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling blue means feeling low, and a true-blue person is a staunch Conservative.

clue.text: Mortal feud ruinous — that's expressed clearly

indicators.note: something ruinous wrecks what it touches, so the letters are wrecked and rebuilt

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A deadly quarrel's ruin is plainly stated.
explanation.definitionFit: To formulate an idea is to put it into precise, systematic words.

clue.text: Party to scowl in misery

blocks.note: a do is a party
to lour is to frown or look sullen

explanation.surface: A political party scowls in its unhappiness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party' tempts as a political one, but a do is a social gathering.
explanation.definitionFit: Dolour is a literary word for grief or sorrow.

clue.text: Punctilious contender from left loading weapon

indicators.note: loading a gun means putting something into it, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: a sticker is slang for a knife or other stabbing weapon
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: An election candidate from the left takes up arms.
explanation.definitionFit: A stickler is a person who insists on exact rules, contending stubbornly for correctness.

clue.text: Is it Chigurh blocking way with extremely scary axe?

indicators.note: extremely means at the extremes, so only the first and last letters are kept
something blocking a route stands inside it, so the way wraps around the rest

blocks.note: a path is a way
the outside letters of the word
to axe is to chop

explanation.surface: A killer with an axe blocking the way asks whether this is Chigurh.
explanation.walkthrough: Anton Chigurh is the murderous hitman in Cormac McCarthy's No Country for Old Men; the question mark marks him as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Chigurh kills without remorse, the textbook case of a person with a severe antisocial personality disorder.

clue.text: Ethics with Starmer questionable — this under present burdens?

indicators.note: something questionable is not in good order, so the letters are put in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Keir Starmer's ethics are questioned while weighed down by the burdens of the moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Present' reads as 'current', but means gifts: the tree is the thing burdened with presents beneath it.
explanation.definitionFit: A decorated fir stands in the home at Christmas with wrapped gifts piled around its base.

clue.text: Drama ending in this literary collection?

blocks.note: describe the final letter of the word drama in words, with an article, rather than taking the letter itself

explanation.surface: A play finishes within an anthology of writing.
explanation.walkthrough: The ending of 'drama' must be described rather than taken: it ends in an A, and 'an A' run together is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Ana is a collection of anecdotes, sayings or gossip about a person, as in Victoriana.

clue.text: Remove from office some unscrupulous Tories

indicators.note: some means only a part, so the letters lie inside the following words

blocks.note: spans the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A call to throw dishonest Conservative MPs out of power.
explanation.definitionFit: To oust someone is to drive them out of a post or position.

clue.text: One must vacate seat daily

indicators.note: to vacate is to leave, so that letter departs from the word

blocks.note: I is one in Roman numerals
a chair is a seat

explanation.surface: An MP must give up their seat every day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Daily' looks like an adverb, but it is the British noun for a cleaner who comes in each day.
explanation.definitionFit: A char, or charwoman, is a cleaner; daily is another British name for the same job.

clue.text: Erica, a PM in 1970s, with monarch then

blocks.note: Edward Heath was UK Prime Minister 1970 to 1974
ER, Elizabeth Regina, the monarch

explanation.surface: A woman named Erica was Prime Minister in the 1970s, alongside the Queen.
explanation.walkthrough: Erica looks like a woman's name, but it is the botanical genus of the plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Erica is the genus name of heath and heather, the low flowering shrubs of moorland.

clue.text: Openly vile lad, as Con, failed us

indicators.note: something that has failed has broken down, so the letters are broken up and rebuilt

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged
taken as written

explanation.surface: A young Conservative's disgraceful conduct has let everyone down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Con' looks like a Conservative here, but it is just three letters of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Scandalous behaviour is shameful and causes public outrage, vile in plain sight.

clue.text: Folk rock boat close to shore: 50 aboard

indicators.note: the close of a word is its final letter, which is the one kept
something aboard a vessel is inside it, so the number goes within the craft

blocks.note: a skiff is a small boat
the last letter of the word
L is 50 in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Fifty people on a little boat rock about near the shore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rock' looks like a boat's motion, but it is part of the music genre.
explanation.definitionFit: Skiffle was 1950s British popular music blending folk, blues and jazz on homemade instruments.

clue.text: Determined detectives brought into action

indicators.note: things brought into something end up inside it

blocks.note: a deed is an action
the Criminal Investigation Department, British police detectives

explanation.surface: Resolute police detectives are called into action.
explanation.definitionFit: Decided and determined both describe a resolute, firm person or a settled outcome.

clue.text: Ill repute to beset Hancock, initially at the top?

indicators.note: something ill is out of sorts, so the letters are put out of order
to beset is to surround, so the word wraps around the letter
initially means at the start, so only the first letter is used

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged
the first letter of the name

explanation.surface: A bad reputation besets Matt Hancock, once near the top of government.
explanation.walkthrough: Matt Hancock was UK Health Secretary until a 2021 scandal damaged his reputation.
explanation.definitionFit: Up there means high up, in a lofty or leading position.

clue.text: Victor in Lab is so composed, one taking bow

indicators.note: one letter goes in among the others
to compose is to put together afresh, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: Victor is V in the NATO phonetic alphabet
the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A Labour winner keeps his composure while taking a bow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taking bow' suggests a victor's applause; it is the bow drawn across strings.
explanation.definitionFit: The bass viol, or viola da gamba, is a stringed instrument played with a bow.

clue.text: In pub the Spanish notice flawed political process

indicators.note: something flawed is imperfect, so these letters must be set right in a new order

blocks.note: a local is one's neighbourhood pub
el is 'the' in Spanish
the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: In a pub, a notice in Spanish criticises a faulty voting process.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain 'your local' is the pub nearest your home.
explanation.definitionFit: A local election chooses councillors for a town or county, one kind of political process.

clue.text: Speak fondly about London police? Wake up!

indicators.note: about means around, so the first word wraps the second

blocks.note: to coo is to murmur lovingly
the Met, London's Metropolitan Police

explanation.surface: Someone murmuring tenderly about the police before shouting at a sleeper.
explanation.definitionFit: To come to is to regain consciousness, so the imperative is an order to wake.

clue.text: Dull affair having no end

indicators.note: with no end means the final letter is cut off

blocks.note: an affair is a matter

explanation.surface: A boring love affair that never stops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Affair' hints at romance, but it is a matter or business.
explanation.definitionFit: A matte surface or finish is dull, without shine or gloss.

clue.text: Sheepish press chief retaining honour after hoax

indicators.note: after places what follows behind, so the deceit comes first in the answer
to retain is to hold within, so the editor holds the other word

blocks.note: a sham is a hoax
the editor runs a newspaper
honour, as in saving or losing face

explanation.surface: A newspaper editor, caught out by a hoax, keeps his dignity but looks embarrassed.
explanation.definitionFit: Shamefaced means visibly embarrassed or guilty, like a sheepish look.

clue.text: See 14
Conservative deception takes in old man, washed up

indicators.note: to take something in is to hold it inside

blocks.note: C is the abbreviation for Conservative
a ruse is a trick
O is the abbreviation for old; 'man' just completes the phrase

explanation.surface: A Tory trick fools an old man whose career is finished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Washed up' reads as finished, but here it is literal: Robinson Crusoe was shipwrecked and washed ashore.
explanation.definitionFit: Defoe's Robinson Crusoe is the archetypal castaway, a man washed up on a desert island.

clue.text: Was leader over summer, having run

indicators.note: over means covering, so the first word sits around the second

blocks.note: led is the past tense of lead
a summer is one who sums, an adder

explanation.surface: Someone who led the party over the summer has stood for office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Summer' is not the season but one who adds up, and 'run' is a ladder in stockings.
explanation.definitionFit: Tights that have a run are laddered, with a vertical line of broken stitches.
